alt: Concentric circles show the primary audience the writer directly addresses at the centre, ringed by a secondary audience who will also read or hear the text. Alongside, broad audiences share little, specialised audiences share expert knowledge, and divided audiences disagree with each other.
caption: Name the group the writer addresses, and a second group where the text supports it.

after: ## What audience tells you about a writer's choices
alt: Four audience features, beliefs, values, needs and background, feed into the writer’s perception, which branches into five choices: diction, evidence, tone, structure and what is left unsaid, each with an example from the lesson.
caption: A writer’s picture of the audience guides almost every choice in the text.

after: ## Evidence of audience in the text
alt: Six numbered cards list clues to audience: direct address, assumed knowledge, shared references, pronouns, anticipated objections, and the publication or setting, each with a short example.
caption: Who a text is for shows in how it addresses, assumes and refers.

alt: A large context panel holds three cards, time, place and occasion, and inside it a smaller box for the exigence, the specific trigger. Below, a solemn occasion calls for brevity and restraint, a rally for emphasis and rhythm, and a party joke would fail at a memorial.
caption: Context is time, place and occasion; the exigence is one trigger within it.

after: ## A public-domain example: Washington in Atlanta (1895)
alt: Washington’s image “Cast down your bucket where you are” reaches three groups: white Southern business and political leaders, Black Southerners, and readers across the country. Below, the context of the Atlanta exposition and the criticism that named it “the Atlanta Compromise”.
caption: A divided audience hears the same words differently, so it shapes every choice.

after: ## Worked example 1: one message, two audiences (written by Marlbridge)
alt: Two versions of the same cancellation notice. Version A, to students, uses plain words such as “fallen through” and leads with the science lab afternoon. Version B, to parents, uses formal phrasing such as “regret to inform you” and covers payments and contact.
caption: Each point ties a feature of the text to a belief or need of its audience.

after: ## Worked example 2: context changes the sentence (written by Marlbridge)
alt: One sentence, “We will not be moved from this square until the vote is taken”, branches into two contexts. For protesters outside a town hall before a vote it is a pledge of resistance; for tourists told the market is closed it is humorous and exaggerated.
caption: The words stay the same; time, place and occasion change their force.
